title: autotrust/JEV-27B: fast, calibrated decisions and full reasoning from one open model
gist: AutoTrust AI released autotrust/JEV-27B, an Apache-2.0 open-weights 'System 1' decision model distilled from the closed TypeSafe Jev 1.13 that edges it on average (84.07 vs 83.85) across six benchmarks while running faster on a single GPU. Its 'Blocks of Experts' recipe adds a 108.9M-parameter LoRA plus decision head to a frozen Qwen3.8-27B, so the same weights also serve untouched System 2 reasoning; cost to build was about 9.2 B200-hours.

themes.theme: Open distillation erodes closed decision-model moat

insights.claim: JEV-27B averages 84.07 versus 83.85 for the hosted closed TypeSafe Jev 1.13 across six public decision benchmarks in the authors' own runs, ahead on 4 of 6 but trailing on Kev (by 1.77) and VitaminC (by 1.00).
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: A closed hosted decision API's differentiation can be replicated by open weights distilled from its own outputs.
insights.quote:
JEV-27B averages 84.07, TypeSafe Jev 1.13 83.85 in our
runs of both

insights.claim: The model was cheap to build: 108.9M trained parameters (0.4% of the backbone) and about 9.2 hours on one B200, trained on Jev's published output distributions from the Apache-2.0 corpus SargeDev/jev-distill-corpus-v3.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Near-zero cost to clone a closed model's behavior undercuts pricing power of specialized hosted models.
insights.quote: Cheap to build: 108.9 M trained parameters (0.4 % of the backbone), ≈ 9.2 hours on one B200.

insights.claim: On 25,376 held-out Jev-labelled questions, mean KL to Jev is about 0.017, meaning an observer needs about 60 sampled decisions to gather one nat of evidence about which model produced them; calibration error is 0.0009 with no post-hoc fix.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Distribution-level fidelity implies the open model is a near drop-in substitute for the closed API in-distribution.
insights.quote: It is calibrated without any post-hoc fix: expected calibration error 0.0009
insights.locator: 2. At the level of probability distributions

insights.claim: On an independent benchmark with human gold labels and no training overlap, JEV-27B reaches 96-98% of Jev's accuracy, versus about 90% for the next-closest models (Laya and zero-shot DeBERTa-v3-large).
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Out-of-distribution parity is close but not complete, bounding how far substitution claims hold.

insights.claim: Distilling from full soft-label probability distributions via KL transfers the teacher's uncertainty along with its answers, so calibration comes for free.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Publishing output probabilities makes a closed model especially easy to distill, a strategic exposure for API vendors.
insights.quote: Distilling it with KL transfers Jev's uncertainty along with its answers, and calibration comes for free.
insights.locator: Why the recipe is so efficient

insights.claim: A faithful student inherits the teacher's blind spots: both models change about 7% of 16-option answers when only option order is shuffled, and on a poker spot Jev shoves with 0.62 versus 0.63 for JEV-27B.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Distilled models replicate errors, so matching a leader is not the same as being correct; risk carries over.
insights.quote: If Jev is wrong about something, assume JEV-27B is wrong about it too.

insights.claim: Instead of fine-tuning a whole LLM into a classifier, the 'Blocks of Experts' recipe keeps Qwen3.8-27B frozen and adds a detachable LoRA r=16 plus a 24-slot decision head, routed per request in one vLLM engine.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Modular adapters on frozen backbones let one deployment serve multiple capabilities, lowering serving costs.
insights.quote:
keep a strong pretrained model frozen as one expert block, and
add a small, detachable block trained for one capability
insights.locator: Two systems, one set of weights

insights.claim: Merging the LoRA into the backbone on the first-generation 9B model dropped HumanEval from 70.7% to 61.6% even though prose perplexity barely moved (3.15 to 3.30); keeping blocks separate preserved HumanEval at 78.0% with byte-identical completions.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Perplexity hides capability loss from fine-tuning merges; adapter separation protects general reasoning.
insights.quote: merging dropped HumanEval from 70.7 % to 61.6 %, a 9-point loss, even though prose perplexity barely moved

insights.claim: Going from 9B to 27B barely changes in-distribution KL (0.019 to 0.017) but more than halves KL on unseen task families (0.234 to 0.104), attributed to intact pretrained knowledge in the frozen backbone.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Backbone scale matters most for generalization, not in-distribution fit, guiding model-size choices for agents.
insights.quote:
it more than halves KL on unseen
task families (0.234 → 0.104)

insights.claim: Agents make many small decisions (phishing, routing, code-rule checks, urgency scoring) that need a fast calibrated probability to threshold on rather than long chain-of-thought, a 'System 1' category the authors say TypeSafe Jev 1.13 popularized.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Points to a distinct, high-volume agent decision layer as a market segment for small, cheap inference.
insights.quote: These questions don't need a long chain of thought.
insights.locator: Agents make a lot of small decisions.

insights.claim: JEV-27B achieves a 137 ms median per decision on one B200 versus 238-301 ms measured for the hosted API, about 130 versus 23 decisions per second, and 4.2 ms per decision batched at 128; the authors caveat that API numbers include network latency.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Self-hosted open models can beat hosted APIs on latency and throughput for high-volume classification.

insights.claim: The authors moved deployment from a B300 to a single H100 80 GB at full bf16 with identical decisions; the H100 delivers 42-54% of a B300's capacity (about 100 vs 220 decisions/s, 64 vs 128 concurrent chats).
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Older-generation H100s remain economically useful for such workloads, supporting their residual value.
insights.quote:
the smaller GPU
costs capacity, not quality
insights.locator: One H100 80 GB, at full bf16 precision.

insights.claim: The authors estimate, untested, that two RTX 5090s with tensor parallelism could fit the bf16 model, while a single RTX 5090 would need FP8 or 4-bit weights.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Consumer GPUs may soon host production-grade decision models, pushing inference toward the edge.
insights.locator: Not yet tested, estimated from memory arithmetic

insights.claim: The authors acknowledge that parity holds inside the training distribution (53 domains), that most comparisons are their own runs pending third-party leaderboard submissions, and that Jev's weaknesses in multi-hop reasoning, arithmetic, counting and adversarial inputs are inherited.
insights.speaker: Josh Liu
insights.so_what: Parity claims remain self-reported; independent verification is the next catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: Matching Jev is not the same as being right.
insights.locator: What "on par" does and doesn't mean
